title: What happens between typing a URL and seeing a page
story:
The question is a standard one and the standard answer is a list. A list is the wrong shape, because it implies every step matters equally, and the useful version of this knowledge distinguishes the steps that cost a journey to the other side of the world from the steps that cost nothing. Count round trips, not stages.

The foundation is old. Cerf and Kahn published A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication in IEEE Transactions on Communications in May 1974, setting out the protocol for interconnecting separate packet networks that became the basis of the internet's transport and addressing layers. Everything below is a consequence of the decision to build on unreliable delivery between independent networks.

Start with the name. The domain name system was specified in RFC 1034 in November 1987 as a distributed, hierarchical database with caching at every level — which means resolution costs a round trip only when no cache along the path already holds the answer. That conditional is the important part: the same page load costs a lookup on a cold cache and nothing on a warm one, so a name resolution is not a fixed item in a latency budget.

Before the name is even used, one step can remove work rather than add it. RFC 6797, of November 2012, specifies HTTP Strict Transport Security, by which a site declares that user agents must interact with it only over secure transport. A user agent holding that declaration rewrites an insecure request locally before sending it — which saves a round trip, and more importantly removes the request an attacker on the path could have intercepted.

Then the connection. RFC 793, of September 1981, specifies the three-way handshake: the initiator sends a segment with the synchronise flag set, the responder answers with synchronise and acknowledge, and the initiator acknowledges. Data may accompany that third message, so establishment costs one full round trip before the first byte of application data can be sent.

Then the encryption, and this is where the numbers have actually changed in living memory. RFC 8446, of August 2018, specifies TLS 1.3, whose full handshake completes in one round trip before application data flows — against two for the previous version. It also defines a zero round trip mode for resumption with a pre-shared key, in which the client sends application data with its very first message. The specification is explicit about the price: such early data is not forward secret against compromise of the pre-shared key, and is not protected against replay between connections. That is the general pattern for every elimination in this list. The round trips are being traded for weaker guarantees, not conjured away.

So a cold connection over the older arrangement costs something like a resolution, plus one journey for the connection, plus one for the encryption, before the server has seen a single byte of the request. Which is what the newer transport attacks. RFC 9000, of May 2021, specifies QUIC, a multiplexed and secure transport over UDP which integrates the cryptographic handshake with transport establishment rather than layering one on the other — so the connection and its encryption are set up together instead of in sequence. RFC 9114, of June 2022, maps HTTP semantics onto it as HTTP/3, where each stream is delivered independently, so losing a packet belonging to one response does not stall the others. That last property is one the earlier multiplexed version could not provide, because it ran many logical streams over a single ordered byte stream and a gap in that stream held everything behind it.

Only after all of that does the server do any work, and only then does the browser parse markup, discover the resources it needs, fetch them, compute layout and paint. Those stages are real and can dominate a slow page — but they are local computation and additional fetches, which behave differently from handshakes and have to be measured differently.

Which gives the diagnostic that makes this knowledge worth having. When a page is slow, the question is not which stage failed but which category the time is in: waiting on a name, waiting on handshakes, waiting on the server to produce the first byte, or waiting on the browser's own main thread. Each has a different fix, and the four are routinely confused by engineers who learned the list and not the budget.

problem.name: The round-trip budget
aka: what happens when you type a URL
problem.shape: A page is slower than it should be and the time is somewhere between the keystroke and the pixels.
tell: the first request to a host is slow and subsequent ones are fast
the server reports a fast response and the user sees a slow page
latency scales with distance rather than with payload size
the diagnosis began with the component the engineer knows best
problem.move: Separate the time into four categories before touching anything: name resolution, connection and encryption handshakes, server time to first byte, and the browser's own parsing and execution. Count the round trips each handshake requires, because only round trips explain latency that scales with distance.
problem.invariant: Each round trip costs the physical time to reach the other party and return, so eliminating one is worth more than any amount of optimisation to the work done between them.
problem.breaks: The counts change with protocol version and the eliminations are purchased rather than free. Zero round trip resumption trades forward secrecy against compromise of the pre-shared key and offers no protection against replay between connections, so a handshake removed from the budget may have moved a risk into the security model instead.

cost.time: measuring four categories separately requires instrumentation at more than one layer, and the browser-side and server-side numbers come from different tools
cost.space: the state that makes the fast paths fast — resolver caches, session tickets, declared transport policies — all of it is cached state that can be stale or absent
cost.beats: reciting the pipeline, which sounds complete and cannot rank anything, and optimising the server alone, which is the one category a server-side metric can see

worked.problem: Trace the latency budget for a first page load: which steps require round trips, and how does the newer transport remove them?
worked.reasoning:
The useful move is to stop listing stages and start counting journeys, because every stage either costs at least one traversal to the other party and back, or costs effectively nothing — and only the first kind can explain latency that grows with distance.

Take them in order. Name resolution may cost a round trip, and may cost nothing: the domain name system was specified in RFC 1034 in November 1987 as a distributed, hierarchical database with caching at every level, so the cost appears only when no cache along the path holds the answer. This is why it is wrong to put a fixed figure for resolution in a budget — the same page load pays for it once and then stops paying.

One step can subtract rather than add. Strict Transport Security, RFC 6797 of November 2012, lets a site declare that user agents must interact with it only over secure transport, and a user agent holding that declaration rewrites an insecure request locally before sending it. That saves a round trip, and more importantly removes the request an on-path attacker could have intercepted.

Connection establishment costs exactly one round trip. RFC 793, of September 1981, specifies the three-way handshake — synchronise, synchronise-acknowledge, acknowledge — and because data may accompany the third message, one full journey elapses before the first application byte can be sent.

The encryption handshake is where the figures have changed recently, and the change is worth quoting precisely. RFC 8446, of August 2018, specifies TLS 1.3, whose full handshake completes in one round trip before application data flows, against two for the previous version. It also defines a zero round trip mode for resumption with a pre-shared key, in which the client sends application data with its first message.

That mode is the one I would be careful about in an interview, because it looks like a free win and the specification says otherwise: early data is not forward secret against compromise of the pre-shared key, and is not protected against replay between connections. That is the general shape of every elimination here — round trips are traded for weaker guarantees, not conjured away — and an engineer who can name the trade is demonstrating something different from one who can name the feature.

So a cold first load over the older arrangement is roughly a resolution, plus one journey for the connection, plus one for the encryption, before the server has seen a byte of the request. Which is precisely what the newer transport attacks. RFC 9000, of May 2021, specifies QUIC over UDP, integrating the cryptographic handshake with transport establishment rather than layering one on the other, so the connection and its encryption are established together instead of in sequence. RFC 9114, of June 2022, maps HTTP onto it as HTTP/3.

There is a second improvement worth more than the handshake saving on a lossy network. Under HTTP/3 each stream is delivered independently, so the loss of a packet belonging to one response does not stall the others. The earlier multiplexed version could not do this: it ran many logical streams over a single ordered byte stream, so a gap held everything behind it, and the multiplexing that was supposed to remove queuing reintroduced it one layer down.

Everything after the first byte is a different kind of time. The server produces a response, the browser parses markup, discovers resources, fetches them, computes layout and paints. Those stages can dominate a slow page, but they are local computation and additional fetches, and they do not scale with distance.

Which is the diagnostic, and it is the reason to learn any of this: when a page is slow the question is not which stage failed but which of four categories holds the time — name resolution, handshakes, server time to first byte, or the browser's own main thread. Each has a different fix, they are routinely confused, and a list of stages gives you no way to tell them apart.

problem.practice: Load a page you have never visited from a network far from its servers, then reload it, and record both times. The difference is what the caches and resumption state were worth. Then find which of the four categories the remaining time is in, using one tool for the browser side and one for the server side.

beats.broke: The pipeline was taught as a list of steps, which gives no way to tell which steps cost anything — so diagnosis proceeded by guessing at whichever component the engineer happened to know best.
beats.fix: Count round trips rather than stages: every step either costs a journey to the other party and back or costs effectively nothing, and only the former explains latency that grows with distance.
beats.cost: The counts change with protocol version and the eliminations are purchased rather than free — zero round trip resumption gives up forward secrecy against a compromised pre-shared key and offers no replay protection between connections.

interview.q: Trace the latency budget for a first page load: which steps require round trips, and how does the newer transport remove them?
interview.trap: Omitting the name resolution or the encryption handshake when estimating setup cost — or presenting zero round trip resumption as free, when the specification states plainly what it gives up.
interview.answer:
Stop listing stages and count journeys, because every stage either costs a traversal to the other party and back or costs effectively nothing, and only the first kind explains latency that grows with distance.

Name resolution costs one round trip or none. RFC 1034, of November 1987, specifies a distributed hierarchical database with caching at every level, so the cost appears only when no cache along the path has the answer — which is why a fixed figure for resolution in a budget is wrong.

One step subtracts. Strict Transport Security, RFC 6797 of November 2012, lets a site declare that agents must use secure transport only, and an agent holding that declaration rewrites the insecure request locally. That saves a trip and, more importantly, removes the request an on-path attacker could have intercepted.

Connection costs exactly one round trip: RFC 793, of September 1981, specifies synchronise, synchronise-acknowledge, acknowledge, and since data may ride the third message, one full journey elapses before the first application byte.

Encryption is where the figures changed. RFC 8446, of August 2018, specifies TLS 1.3 with a full handshake in one round trip before application data, against two previously, plus a zero round trip mode for resumption with a pre-shared key where the client sends data with its first message. I would flag what the specification says about that mode rather than presenting it as free: early data is not forward secret against compromise of the pre-shared key, and is not protected against replay between connections. Every elimination here trades round trips for weaker guarantees.

So a cold load on the older arrangement is a resolution plus one journey for the connection plus one for the encryption before the server sees a byte — which is what QUIC attacks. RFC 9000, of May 2021, integrates the cryptographic handshake with transport establishment over UDP rather than layering one on the other, so connection and encryption are established together; RFC 9114, of June 2022, maps HTTP onto it.

On a lossy network the second improvement matters more than the handshake saving: each stream is delivered independently, so a lost packet in one response does not stall the others. The earlier multiplexed version ran many logical streams over one ordered byte stream, so a gap held everything behind it — the multiplexing meant to remove queuing reintroduced it a layer down.

After the first byte the time is a different kind: server work, parsing, resource discovery, layout, paint. Those can dominate but do not scale with distance. Which gives the diagnostic — the question is never which stage failed but which of four categories holds the time: name, handshakes, server time to first byte, or the browser's main thread. Each has a different fix, and a list of stages cannot tell them apart.

  paint.

takeaway: Answer this question in round trips rather than stages: resolution costs one or none, the connection one, the encryption one — and every elimination, including zero round trip resumption, is purchased with a weaker guarantee the specification names, which is why a slow page is diagnosed by sorting the time into name, handshakes, first byte and main thread rather than by reciting the pipeline.
